**Personhood** — what a person is and what makes one persist — personal identity over time, psychological continuity and what matters in survival, persons as bearers of reasons, rights and responsibility. Not the self, which is self (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics | Dufner (2025), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-ethics/>. A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. It traces these through prudential concern, responsibility, abortion (Marquis), death and brain-death criteria, dementia and advance directives (Dworkin vs Jaworska on Margo), and the separateness of persons (Rawls, Parfit, Nozick, Taurek, Sidgwick, Brink). Its main recurring finding is that the relation that fixes persistence and the relation that matters ethically keep coming apart. It concludes that all three questions remain open. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md)); worth reading as the current, compact reference map from theories of persistence to applied ethics; it is a survey that takes no side, so it is a route to the primary sources (Parfit 1984, Olson 1997, McMahan 2002, Schechtman 1996, Korsgaard 1989) rather than a source of claims. |
| [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md) v2 | The Informational Nature of Personal Identity | Floridi (2011), DOI-10.1007/s11023-011-9259-6. Floridi deflates the diachronic question of personal identity, holding that sameness is always relative to a purpose-fixed level of abstraction and that metaphysical versions of the question "do not deserve to be taken seriously" (p. 554). He puts the synchronic question first: what binds a self's information into a unity. His answer is an admittedly "figurative" 3C model in which the self is the last of three successive encapsulations, corporeal (bonded by chemical bonds), cognitive (bonded by mutual information) and conscious (bonded by semantics, and so dependent on a community). He then reads ICTs as "egopoietic" technologies because they act on all three membranes. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md)); worth reading as the programmatic statement of Floridi's informational, level-of-abstraction approach to the self and its link to his information ethics; its central model is a self-described figure, not an argued theory, and the individuation-first thesis is asserted in a few lines. |
| [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md) v2 | Identification and Identity | Velleman (2002), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/2143.003.0007. Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md)); worth reading as the sharpest critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) identification of autonomy with a volitional essence, and as a careful source for what Frankfurt said in the essays collected in *Necessity, Volition, and Love* (1999). It is not a survey of the 1971–1987 hierarchical account, which it summarizes in one paragraph and defers to "What Happens When Someone Acts?"; its positive view is stated "briefly" and explicitly deferred to other essays. |

| [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md) | Survival and Identity | Lewis (1976), DOI-10.1525/9780520353060-002. What matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness (the R-relation among person-stages), and it is also identity, because the two answers relate different things. Persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the I-relation (being stages of one person) is the R-relation in every possible case. Fission and fusion are two persons sharing stages, counted as one by "tensed identity"; Methuselah is a continuum of overlapping 137-year persons; degrees of personal identity come from supervaluating over cut-offs for R. Against Perry: two persons, not three, took part in a fission. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md)), from a scan of the 1976 printing posted on Andrew M. Bailey's "Papers by David Lewis" page, OCR'd here; worth reading as the four-dimensionalist reconciliation of Parfit with common sense, and the source of stage-sharing and counting by tensed identity. It agrees with Parfit that what matters is mental continuity and connectedness, the R-relation among person-stages, and denies that this conflicts with identity: persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission becomes two persons sharing their early stages, and degrees are handled by supervaluation. A reconciliation by redefinition of counting, which Lewis grants is "somewhat counterintuitive". |
| [LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md) | Personal Identity | Parfit (1971), DOI-10.2307/2184309. Against two beliefs, that every question about personal identity must have an answer and that important questions turn on it. In Wiggins's division case, each half-brain recipient stands in the relation that would be survival if there were only one, so "how could a double success be a failure?". What matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity is one-one and all-or-nothing. Q-memory and q-intention show the relations need not presuppose identity. Speaking of past and future selves by degree of connectedness, the principle of self-interest has no independent force. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Athens course page; worth reading as the paper that separated what matters in survival from identity, and the short original of Part III of Reasons and Persons. Its division case makes "I survive as neither" absurd and "I survive as both" incompatible with identity, so it concludes that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity cannot. It supplies q-memory, the non-branching criterion, and the vocabulary of successive selves. Its first conclusion is argued; its claim that connectedness matters more than continuity is left, in its own words, needing "more arguments than I have space to give". |

| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) | Personal Identity | Olson (2002, rev. 2023), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Separates seven questions (characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology, what matters) and then takes up persistence. Three answers: psychological continuity (the majority view, repaired from Locke's memory criterion via causal dependence), brute-physical continuity (animalism), and anticriterialism. Fission forces the psychological view into multiple occupancy or a non-branching clause, which makes identity not what matters. The too-many-thinkers objection says that if we are not our animals there are two thinkers in every chair. Temporal-parts ontology may leave it indeterminate what we are. Avoids the word "self". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)); worth reading as the standard map of the analytic personal-identity debate, written by the leading animalist. | [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md) | The Self and the Future | Williams (1970), DOI-10.2307/2183946. One experiment, told twice. A and B enter a machine that exchanges their memories and characters, and choose selfishly which emerging person gets $100,000 and which torture: the outcomes make "changing bodies" the natural description. Told as a series of things that will happen to me (amnesia, changed character, another's "memories", then torture), fear stays rational at every step, and the step that completes the swap changes only what happens to someone else. Undecidability and convention make the clash worse, not better. If forced to choose selfishly, pass the pain to the other body, and call it a "risk". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Vermont course page; worth reading as the strongest case that first-person concern tracks the body, and the paper that made the reduplication-free body swap a problem for the psychological view. It tells one body-exchange experiment twice. Told third-personally, with choices before and reactions after, it says A and B swap bodies. Told first-personally, as a series of things that will happen to me before I am tortured, it says I am the one tortured. It argues that neither indeterminacy nor convention can resolve the clash, and ends with a "rather shaky" preference for the bodily answer, as a "risk". An argument from what fear is rational, not a theory. |
| [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Locke (1694), Essay II.xxvii, added in the second edition. Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: the same mass is the same particles, the same oak or horse or man is the same continued life, and the same person is the same consciousness. A person is "a thinking intelligent being" that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches "as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought". It is independent of substance, material or immaterial: the prince's consciousness in the cobbler's body is the same person but not the same man. "Person" is "a forensic term", grounding reward and punishment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md)), in the Wikisource transcription of the 1853 Troutman & Hayes reprint of the sixth-edition text, compared word by word with Project Gutenberg's; worth reading as the founding text of the psychological account of personal identity and the source of the record's whole line on what a person is. It separates the same substance, the same man and the same person, puts the person in "consciousness" extended back to past actions, and calls "person" a "forensic term". Its cases, the prince and the cobbler, the day-man and the night-man, the severed little finger, are argued from intuition, and its key relation, "the same consciousness", is never defined. |

| [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md) | The Sources of Normativity | Korsgaard (1992), Tanner Lectures at Clare Hall, Cambridge. The "normative question" asks what justifies morality's claims on us. Voluntarism, realism and reflective endorsement each fail alone. The answer is autonomy: because human consciousness is reflective, we need reasons, and so need a "conception of your practical identity" that makes us "a law to yourself". Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity". Valuing any identity commits us to valuing our humanity, and reasons are public, so others can obligate us. "Autonomy is the source of obligation." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-465](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-465.md)), as the read substitute for the book The Sources of Normativity (1996, [LIT-599](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-599.md)), which is its "longer version" with commentaries and a reply. Worth reading as Korsgaard's own first statement of practical identity and of the claim that "autonomy is the source of obligation". The reflective structure of human consciousness means we must act for reasons and so must have "a conception of your practical identity", "a description under which you value yourself"; reasons express that identity and obligations "spring from what that identity forbids". Valuing any practical identity commits one to valuing one's humanity, and the publicity of reasons commits one to others. The lectures concede that the argument is "sketchy, and sketchily argued". |

A planning agent governs herself over time when she is self-governing at each time along a planned activity and her intentions at those times interlock like the intentions of people acting together, so that she acts "together" with herself. Her standpoints are "diachronicalized": they include a conditional, reflexive end of her own diachronic self-governance. That end explains how willpower and resisting "shuffling" between incomparable options can be self-governed, and anticipated regret at plan's end rules out drinking Kavka's toxin. | [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard (2014), in Rational and Social Agency: The Philosophy of Michael Bratman (OUP), pp. 190–214. Two conceptions of agency are set side by side: natural (action is movement caused by the right mental state) and normatively constituted (action is movement backed by a unified agent, whose unity is achieved by following norms). Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action "the form of self-determined efficacy". Choosing maxims under that form constitutes one's practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes sets the task of unification. Unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", so people can literally act together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md)), in the author's posted manuscript, not the typeset chapter. Worth reading as the read substitute for Self-Constitution (2009, [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md)), which it summarises and extends, and as Korsgaard's direct engagement with Bratman. Agency is "normatively constituted": an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and that unity is achieved by following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives, which give action "the form of self-determined efficacy". The content of the maxims we choose under that form constitutes our "practical identities". So "we make ourselves into agents", and unity of agency, individual or collective, "is an achievement, not a given". Argued, not proved; the account of reason as unification is said to be "lifted" from her other work. |

Per the publisher's abstract it revisits the Frankfurt–Watson exchange over the structures of free agency, treats it as a debate about self-governance, holds that agential authority comes from an attitude's role in the "Lockean organization" of temporally extended agency rather than from tracking the good, gives that role to self-governing policies, and proposes an intention-based theory. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref and Oxford Academic records, not read. No lawful full text was found: the article is paywalled at the Philosophy Documentation Center (purchase, $20) and the reprint at Oxford Academic, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, and PhilPapers and ResearchGate refused automated requests (403). A human reader with access to Philosophical Topics 32 or to Structures of Agency (pp. 222–253) can read it; that reading would move this to Active and would supply [THEORY-029](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-029.md) with Bratman's self-governing policies first-hand. |
| [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md) | Self-Constitution: Agency, Identity, and Integrity | Korsgaard (2009), Oxford University Press, from her 2002 Locke Lectures. The argument is that we constitute ourselves as agents, and as the particular agents we are, by choosing under the constitutive principles of action, the categorical and hypothetical imperatives. On Plato's "constitutional model", good action is action that issues from a unified soul. The chapters run from agency and identity to "How to be a Person". Unread: registered from the contents; the account is read in [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the Crossref records of the book and its ten chapters, not read: no lawful copy of the book could be reached. Oxford Academic is closed and the Internet Archive scan (selfconstitution0000kors) is an access-restricted lending copy. Korsgaard's drafts of the 2002 Locke Lectures it grew from are no longer on her Harvard site, but survive in the Internet Archive's captures of her old FAS page (people.fas.harvard.edu/~korsgaar/Korsgaard.LL1–LL6, 2002–2005). They are author-posted and lawful, but book-length and superseded, and were not read. Its account is read first-hand in her short restatement "The Normative Constitution of Agency" (2014, [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md), read in full), which extends it. Filed because it is the canonical citation for self-constitution. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied or the drafts are read, not on merit. |

| [LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling (1980), The Public Interest, Summer 1980, pp. 94-118. People behave sometimes "as if they had two selves" in "continual contest for control", and the tactics of self-management (removing the option, bright lines, monitoring, delays, raising the stakes) are the tactics of managing someone else. A single-dimension model of impatience fits poorly. Which self is authentic is left open. Failures of consumer self-management may be worth "on the order of a trillion dollars". | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md)), in place of the 1984 Ely Lecture ([LIT-573](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-573.md)), which has no lawful free copy. Worth reading as Schelling's own first statement of "egonomics": a person sometimes behaves "as if they had two selves" that alternate in command, and the tactics people use on themselves (mittens, alarm clocks across the room, bright lines, Christmas savings, deadlines, delays) are the tactics they use to manage another person. It refuses to say which self is authentic in general, and it gives an order-of-magnitude estimate that failures of consumer self-management cost as much as all other consumer-ignorance problems together. |
| [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |
